author: Robert Salesas’ profile
text:
184,000 tech workers have been laid off in 2026. Across 247 events. That's 1,143 people per day, every day, since January 1.

The staggering part: 55% of those layoff announcements explicitly cite AI, automation, or machine learning as the driving factor. That's 152,000 people whose termination letters essentially say "a model can do your job now."

Except that's not entirely true.

Oxford Economics concluded in January that firms "don't appear to be replacing workers with AI on a significant scale." Sam Altman — the CEO of the company most associated with AI displacement — told CNBC there's "some AI washing where people are blaming AI for layoffs that they would otherwise do."

So what's actually happening? Both things simultaneously. Companies are cutting roles in customer support, content moderation, data entry, QA testing, and traditional software engineering. They're redirecting the payroll savings into a collective $700 billion AI infrastructure buildout. Developers using AI coding tools produce 40-55% more code per sprint. New software engineering job postings are down 15% compared to the same period in 2025.

The industry is using AI as both the reason to fire and the reason to hire. Cut 10 support agents, hire 2 AI engineers. Reduce the QA team by half, double the ML ops budget. The net headcount drops. The total payroll sometimes doesn't.

Here's the uncomfortable truth for anyone sitting in a senior tech role: the question isn't whether AI is replacing workers. It's that "AI is replacing workers" has become such a convenient narrative that companies are using it as cover for ordinary cost-cutting — and the people who actually are being displaced by AI can't tell the difference from the ones who were just unlucky.

Both groups get the same LinkedIn post from their former CEO about "difficult decisions" and "the future of work."

ML Failure Analysis #02.

Across the mid-market AI programs we have audited in the last 18 months, the failure modes cluster into 5 patterns. Four of the 5 are operational, not technical. Programs survive or get cut in the budget cycle based on these 5, not on model accuracy.

Failure 1: No business metric paired with the model metric. The model engineer reports AUC. The business reports revenue. Nobody connects the two. Six months in, the AUC is up and the revenue is flat, and nobody can defend why the model deserves another quarter of investment. The fix is to define both metrics at deployment time and put them on the same dashboard.

Failure 2: Silent drift with no monitoring. The model that worked in Q1 will drift in Q3. Most teams discover this through customer complaints in Q4. By then the program has shipped wrong outputs for 3 to 4 months. The fix is the 4-metric drift framework from OASIS #97: input distribution shift, prediction distribution shift, performance on labeled slice, business KPI drift. Under $30 a month to implement.

Failure 3: Train-serve skew. The model performs in evaluation and fails in production because the input pipeline at serving time computes features differently than the training pipeline. 🚀 Day 19 of My Machine Learning Learning Journey
🤔 Did you know there are TWO ways to use a pretrained model?
Last time, we talked about Transfer Learning and how we don't always need to build an AI model from scratch.
But while exploring it further, I discovered something interesting.
Most beginners (including me when I first started) think there's only one way to use a pretrained model.
There isn't.
There are actually two common approaches, and choosing the right one depends on your dataset and your problem.
So let's break them down.
1️⃣ Feature Extraction
Imagine you've hired an experienced photographer. 
Instead of teaching them photography again, you simply ask them to take pictures for your project.
You trust the skills they already have.
That's Feature Extraction.
The pretrained model already knows how to identify useful features like edges, textures, shapes, and patterns.
So we freeze all of its learned layers and only train the final classification layer for our dataset.
It's fast, efficient, and works really well when your dataset is small.
2️⃣ Fine-Tuning
Now imagine the same photographer starts working in wildlife photography after years of shooting weddings.
They already know photography...
but they still need to adapt to a completely different environment.
That's Fine-Tuning.
Instead of freezing the entire model, we allow some of the deeper layers to learn from our new dataset.
This helps the model become more specialized for our specific task.
📊 The workflow in the image shows both approaches.
Sometimes simply replacing the last layer is enough.
Other times, retraining a few deeper layers gives much better results.
The trick is knowing when to use each approach.
📚 Today's takeaway
What Feature Extraction is
What Fine-Tuning is
The difference between the two
When each approach is useful
💡 My biggest takeaway
One thing I've learned while revisiting these concepts is that Machine Learning isn't always about choosing the most complex solution.
Sometimes, freezing a model is enough.
Sometimes, fine-tuning gives better performance.
Knowing which approach fits your problem is just as important as knowing how to build the model itself.
That's exactly why I continue this series.
Not just to revise the basics, but to understand the decisions that real ML engineers make while building AI systems.
🌱 One concept at a time.

author: Olive Nwaigbo
text:
The $2M Feature Nobody Asked For. ❌

A fintech startup once raised a Series A on the strength of a single slide: 
"AI-Powered Expense Categorization." 

Investors loved it. Users didn't.

Turns out the "AI" was just an if-else ladder wearing a trench coat. 

The real pain point, reconciling expenses across currencies,  was still a manual spreadsheet nightmare. Eighteen months later, they had to pivot the entire product. 

Not because AI failed them. 
But because they never had an AI product. They had a normal product with an AI garnish.

This mix-up happens every day. Here is how to tell the difference:

🤖 AI-Powered Products (AI as a Feature)
These are products that can exist without AI, but use it to sharpen a specific step. 
• Think: Spotify’s Discover Weekly or Gmail’s Smart Compose. 
• If you remove the AI tomorrow, the core product still stands, it’s just a little duller.
• For PMs: This is a feature bet. Prove the lift on retention, define a fallback, and iterate.

⚡ AI Products (AI as the Product)
These cannot exist without the model. The AI *is* the value proposition.
• Think: ChatGPT, Midjourney, or GitHub Copilot. 
• There is no stripped-down "manual mode" underneath.
• For PMs: This changes the entire game. You have to define quality for unpredictable outputs and manage roadmaps gated by models you don’t control.

Why It Matters:
Confusing the two shows up fast. It breaks your team structure (bolting on one ML engineer vs. making model work your core discipline) and ruins your metrics.

Before writing "AI" on your roadmap, ask yourself: 
Would this product still deliver its core value if the AI disappeared tomorrow?

• Yes? → You have an AI-powered feature. Treat it like any other feature.
• No? → You have an AI product. Change your metrics, your team, and your definition of quality.

Neither is better. But conflating them is how you raise money on a slide your users never needed.

Where are you building right now — AI-powered, or AI-native? How is that shaping your roadmap? 👇

• Shared tooling, linting, and CI config live once, not N times  
• Refactoring is trivial grep, rename, done. No cross-repo version-bump hell  
• Single source of truth for dependency versions kills "works on my repo" drift  

Bottlenecks  
• CI gets slow fast without a smart build graph (Bazel, Nx, Turborepo) you're rebuilding the world on every push  
• Git itself starts to strain at scale clone times, blame history, LFS creep  
• Access control gets messy hard to give a vendor or contractor scoped access to just one service  
• Org-wide blast radius one bad merge can block every team, not just one  

𝗠𝗨𝗟𝗧𝗜-𝗥𝗘𝗣𝗢  
Benefits  
• Clean ownership boundaries each team ships, versions, and deploys independently  
• Small, fast CI pipelines scoped to one service  
• Forces API-first thinking you can't cheat and reach into another service's internals  
• Easier to open-source or externalize a single component  

Bottlenecks  
• Dependency hell a breaking change across 12 repos means 12 PRs, 12 review cycles, 12 release trains  
• Tooling and config drift every repo slowly diverges without heavy investment in shared templates  
• Cross-cutting refactors (rename a field, bump a shared lib) become a project, not a commit  
• Discoverability suffers new engineers don't know where to look  

𝗠𝗬 𝗧𝗔𝗞𝗘  
There's no universally "correct" answer it's a function of team topology, deployment cadence, and how tightly your services are coupled. What's worked best in practice: monorepo within a bounded platform/domain (e.g., all AI platform services), multi-repo across domains with genuinely independent lifecycles. The real unlock isn't the repo structure itself. It's investing early in build-graph tooling (Nx, Bazel, Turborepo) and CI caching that's what decides whether a monorepo scales gracefully or collapses under its own weight. Curious how others are handling this, especially in AI/ML platform teams where services and pipelines multiply fast. What's your setup and would you choose differently if you started over?

Mike Cohen's 50 ML Projects to Understand LLMs uses hands-on experiments to examine tokenization, embeddings, output logits, hidden states, attention heads, and MLP layers.

Many projects go beyond visualizing model internals. You use statistical tests, controls, activation patching, head ablation, and neuron lesioning to test what changes the model’s behaviour.

All 50 projects run in Google Colab. Each includes a partial notebook for guided practice and a complete solution. Most can run on a standard CPU, although a GPU speeds up some larger experiments.

The book relies heavily on GPT-2, alongside BERT, and older transformers. That makes the models easier to inspect, but the coverage leans towards older model families rather than current frontier LLMs.

You’ll need some Python. Basic algebra is enough to begin, while familiarity with machine learning, statistics, and linear algebra will help with the harder projects.

The focus is model internals, not RAG, agents, deployment, or LLM application development.

A typical OpenShift bare metal deployment includes bootstrap, control plane (master), worker nodes, DNS, load balancer, networking, and storage configuration. Organizations can choose between User-Provisioned Infrastructure (UPI) for greater flexibility or Installer-Provisioned Infrastructure (IPI) where supported.

Successful deployments require careful planning around networking, load balancing, storage, and cluster architecture. Common challenges include DNS configuration, bootstrap failures, ignition files, certificates, and node communication.

I get asked this a lot:
“Do I need a deep ML background to become an AI Engineer?”
If it was 2023 or even 2024, I would have probably said yes.

Because most AI work was still closer to model training, experimentation, research, data science, and ML pipelines.

But in 2026, my answer is different.

Not because ML fundamentals are unimportant.
They are still important.

But the role of an AI Engineer has changed.
Today, most companies are not asking engineers to build foundation models from scratch.

They are asking engineers to build useful systems around models.
That means knowing how to:

Connect LLMs to real business data
Design RAG pipelines
Handle context properly
Build tool-calling workflows
Add memory where it actually helps
Route between models
Control cost and latency
Add guardrails
Evaluate outputs
Monitor failures
Deploy safely
This is the part many people underestimate.

AI Engineering is becoming less about “Can you train the model?”
And more about:

“Can you turn the model into a reliable product?”

That is a very different skill set.

You still need to understand tokens, embeddings, context windows, sampling, inference, evals, and model behavior.

But you do not need to wait until you become a research scientist to start.

My advice is simple:
Pick one real problem.
Build a small AI app.
Add retrieval.
Add tools.
Add guardrails.
Add evals.
Deploy it.
Break it.
Improve it.
Repeat.

That is how you become an AI Engineer in 2026.

🚀 Project 10: End-to-End ML Workflow — From Raw Data to Responsible AI in Production


As part of my Data Science Internship at LinuxWorld Informatics Pvt Ltd., I explored what it truly takes to build Machine Learning solutions that are ready for the real world.

One thing I realized during this project is that Machine Learning isn't just about training a model. A successful AI solution requires quality data, the right algorithms, proper evaluation, and responsible deployment.

This project helped me understand the complete lifecycle of an ML system—from raw data to ethical AI.

📊 Stage 1: Data
Everything starts with data.
I learned how to:
✅ Define the business problem
✅ Collect data from multiple sources
✅ Handle missing values, duplicates, and outliers
✅ Perform Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
✅ Engineer meaningful features
✅ Create Train, Validation & Test datasets
Key takeaway: Better data leads to better models.

🤖 Stage 2: Model Development
I explored different algorithms including:
• Logistic Regression
• Decision Trees
• Random Forest
• XGBoost
• Neural Networks
I also learned about:
✔ Cross Validation
✔ Hyperparameter Tuning
✔ SMOTE for imbalanced datasets
✔ Model Persistence using Pickle/Joblib
Key takeaway: The best model isn't always the most complex one.

📈 Stage 3: Model Evaluation
A model should perform well on unseen data, not just the training set.
I explored evaluation using:
• Accuracy
• Precision
• Recall
• F1 Score
• ROC-AUC
• Confusion Matrix
• MAE, RMSE & R²
Along with model comparison and error analysis to understand where predictions fail.
Key takeaway: Evaluation builds confidence before deployment.

⚖️ Stage 4: Responsible AI
This was my favorite part because AI should be trustworthy.
I explored:
🔹 Fairness & Bias Detection
🔹 Explainable AI (SHAP & LIME)
🔹 Privacy & Compliance
🔹 Human-in-the-Loop Systems
🔹 Ethical Deployment Practices
Key takeaway: Responsible AI is just as important as accurate AI.

🌟 What I Learned
This project gave me a much broader perspective on how Machine Learning is applied in production environments. It strengthened my understanding of data preparation, model development, evaluation techniques, and the importance of building AI systems that are transparent, reliable, and aligned with business goals.

Grateful to LinuxWorld Informatics Pvt. Ltd. and my mentors for this valuable learning experience.

I've read a few hundred FDE job posts this year. The thing they screen for in the loop is almost never the thing candidates prepare for.

Here's the tell: the highest-paying FDE roles ask for the fewest years. Physical Intelligence wants a Forward Deployed Robotics Engineer with 2 years. Modal asks 2 years of ML for a seat paying up to $250K + equity. ElevenLabs literally says "customers in student clubs count."

That's not a low bar. It's a different bar. They've stopped screening for résumé and started screening for evidence you can do the actual job — which is three things:

Can you take a half-formed, contradictory customer ask and scope it into something shippable, live, without a PM in the room?

Can you build a working demo under time pressure while a non-technical stakeholder watches — and read whether they're actually sold?

When the deployment breaks in production at the customer's site, do you own it end to end, or do you file a ticket and wait?

None of that shows up on LeetCode. It shows up in stories: "here's a messy integration I owned from first call to go-live." That's what a good FDE interviewer is fishing for, and it's why frontier labs pay $350–550K+ for people who can prove it.

If you're prepping for an FDE loop: bring three of those stories, not three algorithms.

Hiring managers — what's the one signal that tells you a candidate can actually survive in front of a customer?

author: Waleed El-Naggar
text:
Information Security Role in AI era:

Information Security isn't just getting new tools. It's getting a new job description.

For years, the job was: protect the perimeter, patch the vulnerabilities, control who logs in. That's still true. But AI is adding a whole new layer that most security teams weren't hired to handle.

A few things I keep seeing play out:

- We're defending systems that don't behave the same way twice. An LLM can be "tricked" through language itself — prompt injection, jailbreaks, subtle manipulation. There's no patch for that the way there's a patch for a known exploit.

- Access control isn't just about people anymore. AI agents are booking meetings, writing code, sending emails on our behalf. The real question isn't "who can log in" — it's "what is this agent actually allowed to do, and what happens if it's fooled into doing more."

- The attackers are using AI too. Phishing emails are more convincing. Social engineering is faster and cheaper to run at scale. The average attack just got a lot more sophisticated, and it didn't take a nation-state to do it.

- Security engineers are quietly becoming ML-literate. Understanding embeddings, fine-tuning, and RAG pipelines is turning into table stakes, the same way understanding networking was 15 years ago.

The honest summary: the job is moving from "harden a fixed perimeter" to "govern a system that's constantly learning, adapting, and occasionally being manipulated in ways you didn't anticipate."
That's a harder job. It's also a more interesting one.

Curious how others in security are seeing this shift — are you building new playbooks, or stretching old ones to fit?

text:
This Summer, I Turned Engineer.

Not because I earned a degree.
Because I stopped letting my specialization define my limits.

I walked into this summer convinced I knew what kind of engineer I wanted to become. I walked out with a completely different definition of engineering.
It started with a job interview that wasn't even mine. A candidate mentioned: "I checked your website before coming here, but I couldn't find the information I was looking for." Then someone looked at me and asked: "Can you build us a better website?"

My first thought? Of course not. I'm an AI/ML guy. 😭

An entire production web platform? Not my field. Still, I said yes.

Somewhere between "I have no idea how to build this" and actually deploying it, I realized three things:
• Engineering isn't about being an expert in one field.
• You never know which skill the next problem will demand.
• In a world moving this fast, the most important skill is the ability to learn.

Every time I solved one problem, the project handed me another. Strangely, I stopped seeing that as a setback. It became my favorite part of the process.

And the deeper I went, the more I realized the problem wasn't just an outdated website. It was a static system. New product? Change the code. New project? Change the code. New job opening? Change the code.

So I stopped thinking about building pages. I started thinking about building a system.

What began as a simple website rewrite became a complete digital platform. Today, the platform powers product management, projects, careers, certificates, client showcases, and an AI assistant, all built on a custom CMS for the company's day-to-day operations.

And then my AI brain kicked in. 😅

I built a domain-specific RAG assistant using the company's technical knowledge base. The hardest part wasn't the LLM. It was turning years of 
messy documents into knowledge a machine could actually understand.

Cleaning.
Structuring.
Chunking.
Embedding.
Retrieving.
Reranking.

And teaching the assistant something surprisingly important: Knowing when not to answer. Because a trustworthy answer is far more valuable than a confident hallucination.

Looking back, AI made me faster. It didn't make the decisions.

It didn't decide that a CMS made more sense than a static website. It didn't decide how the AI assistant should behave. Those weren't coding problems. They were engineering decisions.

AI can write code.
Engineers decide why, what, and whether to build it at all.

The problem never cared what I already knew. It only cared whether I was willing to learn what it needed.

Turns out, engineering isn't the degree I chose. It's the mindset I found.

Curious? Here's what that summer turned into: www.wellmangroup.in
And I’d love to know what you think. Explore it, break it, critique it. I’m all ears. 👀

author: Mohammad Khir
text:
The most tedious part of an ML engineer's job?

An AI agent just did 700 rounds of it in 2 days — and beat the human baseline.

Andrej Karpathy showed an "autoresearch" agent that ran 700 experiments on its own to optimize training code. Result: an 11% speedup. People are already calling it "The Karpathy Loop."

The first reaction is fear. "That's my job."

I think that's the wrong read.

Here's what actually got automated: the grind. The tweak-run-measure-repeat loop nobody enjoys anyway.

Here's what did NOT get automated:
→ knowing which 700 experiments are worth running
→ framing the problem so the metric means something
→ deciding the 11% is even the right thing to chase

The agent optimized the search.
It didn't decide what to search for.

That's the shift I'd bet my career on: the value moves from running the work to directing it. From executing loops to asking the right question before the loop starts.

If your whole value is doing the tedious part faster than the next person — that's the part getting commoditized.

If your value is judgment about what's worth building — you just got a very fast intern.

So I'm curious where you land:

Is the Karpathy Loop a threat to engineers, or the best junior teammate we've ever had?

📦 𝗴𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗱𝗱

author: Luis Jimenez Rubia
text:
An interesting observation from recent discussions with data engineers across various companies is that almost nobody is running a single-platform data stack anymore.

Most mid-to-large organizations are utilizing a combination of:

→ Databricks for ML and large-scale processing  
→ Snowflake or BigQuery for analytics  
→ Microsoft Fabric for business user self-service  
→ PostgreSQL or similar for operational data  
→ dbt sitting on top of one or more of these  
→ Power BI or Tableau for visualization  

This trend is not a failure of strategy but rather a reflection of how data platforms evolve in real organizations. Different teams adopt different tools at various times, and the cost of migration makes consolidation unrealistic.

The critical question has shifted from "which platform should we choose?" to "how do we govern data quality, lineage, and access across platforms?"

The skills that are becoming increasingly important include:

→ Federated query patterns (knowing when to push compute vs. pull data)  
→ Cross-platform lineage tracking (Collibra, OpenLineage, dbt’s exposures)  
→ Identity and access management that works across stacks  
→ Cost monitoring that aggregates across vendors  
→ Defining clear ownership for each platform without creating silos  

The data engineer of 2020 needed to master one stack. The data architect of 2026 needs to design for the reality that there will always be three.

How is your organization handling multi-platform governance?

author: Bogdan Kuts’ profile
text:
The AI skills gap is not about AI.

Everyone is hiring AI engineers. Almost nobody is hiring the people who make AI actually work. Companies recruit machine learning specialists and prompt engineers, then the project stalls. Not because the model is wrong, but because nobody can deploy it properly.

The real gap is software engineering: data pipeline design, infrastructure that handles variable load, monitoring that catches quality degradation, error handling for systems that fail in ways traditional software never does.

Our strongest AI teams are majority traditional software engineers. One or two people focus on the model. Everyone else builds the system around it. A mortgage company came to us after their AI intake system, built by ML specialists, kept crashing under load. The model was excellent. The infrastructure was a prototype on a single server with no monitoring. We rewrote the surrounding system, kept the model, and cut loan prep time from four hours to 25 minutes.

Nineteen years of production software taught us something the AI industry is still learning: the model is five percent of the system. The other ninety-five percent is just engineering.

author: Aarsh Desai, open to work
text:
I spent the last few weeks building a chest X-ray classifier, and the most useful thing I learned had nothing to do with the model.

It was this: in this dataset only about 4.5% of the labels are positive. So a model that predicts "nothing wrong" every single time scores 95% accuracy while being completely useless. Accuracy is a trap. Switching to macro-AUROC as my metric made the whole project more honest, and that reframing drove every decision after it.

What I built: a model that detects 14 findings (effusion, cardiomegaly, pneumothorax, and others) from a single frontal chest X-ray, trained on the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset with custom PyTorch training loops.

A few results I'm happy with:
• A from-scratch CNN got 0.60 test AUROC. Swapping in DenseNet-121 with transfer learning took it to 0.80, and that one change also cut the gap between validation and test performance by more than half.
• Tuning a separate decision threshold per disease, instead of a flat 0.5, raised the F1 score from 0.13 to 0.30.

But the part I'm most proud of isn't a number. I ran a Grad-CAM audit to check whether the model was actually reading the lungs or just keying off the text markers in the corner of the image. It passed: attention centered on the heart for cardiomegaly and spread to the lung edges for the diffuse findings, which is where you'd actually look.

It's live if you want to try it. Upload an X-ray, and you get per-finding predictions plus a heatmap of where the model looked. Built with PyTorch, deployed on Streamlit.

To be clear, this is a portfolio project, not a medical device. But it taught me how to evaluate a model honestly, which feels a lot like the actual job.

author: Timur Spiridonov
text:
A few years ago I kept hearing the same complaint from agencies and pharma marketers during customer discovery calls: the DMP pharma segments everyone was buying ran on 30-day cookies and didn't separate by condition at all. 
You'd buy "pharma audience" and basically get someone who might still care, might not.
I figured we could do better if our engineers built an ML model that actually read the content on SSP pages instead of relying on tags — catching people genuinely reading about symptoms, conditions, treatment options. Kept it OTC-focused on purpose.
The harder part was identity. We ended up building our own synthetic stable ID (Otclick ID) so we could follow the same person across sessions and devices, then spent a while mapping out a taxonomy across 73 different conditions.
Then it was just months of grinding — tuning CR, CTR, PI campaign by campaign against forecast. Brands of Nise, Omez, Polysorb, Prostanorm, Oki. Most beat plan on CR by somewhere between 2x and 9x, PI usually 20-40% above forecast.
It was only then that I began to really promote this idea in the market — first within advertising agencies, from directors of partner relations and traffic procurement right through to directors of client groups and industry verticals, and then to the heads of digital divisions within the pharmaceutical companies themselves.
Honestly, the algorithm was never the hard part. Proving "relevant" campaign after campaign was.
